# Sela Sutta (Snp 3.7 (PTS Snp 102))
**ID:** Snp 3.7 (PTS Snp 102)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Sela Sutta* (Snp 3.7; PTS Snp 102) is a mixed prose-and-verse discourse belonging to the *Mahāvagga* of the *Suttanipāta* [Norman 1983; Winternitz 1933]. The narrative relates the encounter between the Buddha and the brāhmaṇa Sela, who approaches to ascertain whether the Buddha possesses the thirty-two physical marks of a great man (*mahāpurisa*) [Norman 1983]. Because two of these marks are hidden, the Buddha exercises supernormal powers to reveal his broad tongue and sheath-encased organ to Sela [Norman 1983; Anālayo 2017]. Impressed by these signs, Sela recites verses of praise and urges the Buddha to rule mankind as a "king of kings" (*rājābhirāja*); the Buddha responds by affirming his status as a spiritual king who turns the wheel of the Dhamma [SuttaCentral; Endo 1997]. Convinced, Sela and his assembly of students take ordination and subsequently attain arahantship [Anālayo 2017].
The text is identical in content to *Majjhima Nikāya* 92 (*Sela Sutta*), and its verse portion is preserved independently in the *Theragāthā* (Thag 16.6, *Selattheragāthā*) [Norman 1983; SuttaCentral]. Its opening narrative concerning the ascetic Keṇiya parallels the Vinaya *Bhesajjakkhandhaka* (Kd 6), which scholars note presents a shorter version lacking the Sela episode [Katre 1931; DharmaNexus]. Computationally, DharmaNexus records massive internal reuse with MN 92 (over 22,000 shared characters, similarity 0.98), Kd 6, and texts sharing standard descriptions of the thirty-two marks such as the *Brahmāyu Sutta* (MN 91) and *Ambaṭṭha Sutta* (DN 3) [DharmaNexus]. Outside Pali, a parallel appears in the Chinese *Ekottarika-āgama* (EA 49.6) as well as the Sanskrit *Mahāvastu*, with related passages in the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya (*Bhaiṣajyavastu* and *Saṅghabhedavastu*) [SuttaCentral; Anālayo 2017; DharmaNexus]. Northern sources, such as the *Divyāvadāna*, cite the *Sailagāthā* alongside the *Arthavarga* and *Munigāthā* as a recognized early scriptural text [Hazra 1994; Lamotte 1988].
